article.excerpt: In Hindi and Indian English, "propose karna" means confessing romantic interest and asking someone to be your partner — not asking them to marry you. Propose Day 2027 is Monday 8 February. Here is the verb, the contact mechanism behind the shift, and which sense you actually mean.

keyTakeaways: In Hindi and Indian English, propose karna means confessing romantic interest and asking someone to be your girlfriend or boyfriend — the marriage sense has to be marked explicitly with शादी.

faqs.question: Does propose karna mean a marriage proposal in Hindi?
faqs.answer: Usually not. Left unmarked, प्रपोज़ करना (propose karnā) means confessing romantic interest and asking someone to be your girlfriend or boyfriend. For the marriage sense you have to mark it — शादी के लिए प्रपोज़ करना, 'to propose for marriage'.

faqs.question: How do you say "will you be my girlfriend" in Hindi?
faqs.answer: क्या तुम मेरी गर्लफ्रेंड बनोगी? — Kyā tum merī girlfriend banogī? The -ogī ending is for a female addressee; a male addressee takes बनोगे (banoge). The तुम register here is familiar, which is what this ask normally assumes.

faqs.question: Why do Indians say "I proposed her" instead of "I proposed to her"?
faqs.answer: Because the Hindi frame carries over. मैंने उसे प्रपोज़ किया takes a direct object with no preposition, and Indian English keeps that structure and drops the 'to'. It is idiomatic in Indian English, not an error inside that variety.

faqs.question: What date is Propose Day in 2027?
faqs.answer: Monday 8 February 2027. It is the second of the eight dated days of Valentine week, which runs from Rose Day on Sunday 7 February to Valentine's Day on Sunday 14 February.

faqs.question: Is Propose Day the first day of Valentine week?
faqs.answer: No — Rose Day on 7 February is first and Propose Day is second. Valentine week is eight dated days, not seven, counting Valentine's Day itself.

faqs.question: What is the difference between रिश्ता and प्रपोज़ करना?
faqs.answer: रिश्ता (riśtā) is a marriage match arranged between families — रिश्ता आना, 'for a match to come'. प्रपोज़ करना is something one person does to another. They are not synonyms and are almost never used of the same event.

faqs.question: Should I use तुम or आप when proposing in Hindi?
faqs.answer: तुम for a peer or someone you are already close to, आप where the relationship or the family setting calls for respect, तू only in genuinely intimate or non-honorific usage. Hindi marks register on the pronoun and the verb ending together, so the choice changes करोगी to करेंगी.

faqs.question: Is the Indian meaning of "propose" recorded in dictionaries?
faqs.answer: Not in the open reference works we checked. English Wiktionary's entry for propose lists three verb senses — suggest a plan, ask for a person's hand in marriage, intend — and none is labelled for India or covers the 'ask someone to be your partner' sense.

faqs.question: How did an English verb like propose become a Hindi verb?
faqs.answer: Through the light verb strategy: Hindi nominalises the borrowed verb and puts the inflection on करना, 'to do'. A typology drawn from over 60 languages lists Hindi borrowing from English among the languages that use this pattern, and the same pattern gives clean karnā and adjust karnā.

faqs.question: Does anyone know when Propose Day started?
faqs.answer: We could not find a source that says. No peer-reviewed work we searched documents when or where Propose Day began, or treats Valentine week's day-by-day structure as a documented South Asian elaboration, so this page states no origin.

faqs.question: What should I send if I only want to say I love you, not propose marriage?
faqs.answer: A declaration rather than a question. मुझे तुमसे प्यार है (Mujhe tumse pyār hai) needs no yes-or-no button, and the 'I love you' page is the template built for that sense — it is the second most-built page type on the platform at 1,173 pages, 23.2% of everything created.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Propose Day Meaning in Hindi: What Propose Karna Means

The propose day meaning in Hindi that people are actually searching for is a meaning of a verb, not of a date. In Hindi and in Indian English, **प्रपोज़ करना (propose karnā) means telling someone you love them and asking them to be your girlfriend or boyfriend — it does not mean asking them to marry you.** Propose Day falls on **Monday 8 February 2027**, and that shifted verb is why the day is a day of confessions rather than engagements.

SubhSandesh's own usage points the same way: across 5,061 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, spread over 20 page types, the second most-built type is the "I love you" page (/love-gf) at 1,173 pages, 23.2% of everything created. That same template is also the most-viewed, at 16,902 views, 30.1% of all page views. Below: the verb, how it shifted, and which sense you mean.

## What "propose karna" means in Hindi

**प्रपोज़ करना (propose karnā) is a Hindi verb phrase meaning "to declare romantic interest and ask someone to become your partner".** It is the English verb *propose* carried into Hindi and conjugated with the light verb करना (*karnā*, "to do"), and in ordinary speech it does not carry the British or American sense of asking for someone's hand in marriage.

The marriage sense exists in Hindi, but it has to be marked. You say शादी के लिए प्रपोज़ करना (*śādī ke liye propose karnā*, "to propose for marriage") or you drop the loanword entirely and say शादी (*śādī*, "marriage"). Left bare, प्रपोज़ करना is read as a confession.

A third word occupies the slot English speakers usually reach for. A marriage proposal arranged between families is रिश्ता (*riśtā*), "a relation" or "a match" — रिश्ता आना, "for a match to come". रिश्ता and प्रपोज़ करना are not synonyms.

This is also why the Indian English sentence *"I proposed her"* is idiomatic here and ungrammatical to a British ear. The Hindi is मैंने उसे प्रपोज़ किया (*Maine use propose kiyā*, "I proposed to her/him"), where the verb takes default third-person masculine singular agreement because the object is case-marked — the pattern set out in the [2019 Hindi light-verb analysis in *Linguistic Issues in Language Technology*](https://journals.colorado.edu/index.php/lilt/article/view/1419). Indian English keeps the Hindi frame and drops the *to*.

## How an English verb becomes a Hindi verb

Hindi does not conjugate borrowed English verbs directly. It nominalises them and hangs the inflection on a native "do" verb — the pattern linguists call the **light verb strategy**. Wichmann and Wohlgemuth's [typology of loan verbs](https://www.linguist.de/jw/Wichmann_Wohlgemuth_verb-borrowing-typology.pdf), drawn from over 60 languages in 72 donor–recipient combinations, sets out four strategies for borrowing a verb and lists *Hindi [Indo-Aryan] < English* among the languages that use the light verb one.

The 2019 *LiLT* analysis says the same from the Hindi side: light verbs in Hindi "can combine with another verb, an adjective, adverb or even a borrowed English verb or noun", and this kind of complex predication is "highly productive" in Hindi and other South Asian languages.

You hear it everywhere once you notice it: क्लीन करना (*clean karnā*, "to clean"), एडजस्ट करना (*adjust karnā*, "to adjust"), कैंसिल करना (*cancel karnā*). English Wiktionary's usage note on [करना](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%A4%95%E0%A4%B0%E0%A4%A8%E0%A4%BE) records the rule plainly: in [Hinglish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinglish), English verbs are conjugated as compound verbs with करना.

Borrowing the form, though, is not the same as borrowing the meaning. A study of French loanwords in Persian published in *Acta Linguistica Asiatica* in 2013 examined [1,878 borrowed items and found 330 of them had undergone a type of semantic change](https://journals.uni-lj.si/ala/article/view/219) — roughly one in six.

Closer to home, a study of English loanwords in Midnapuri Bengali documents [*massacre* shifting to mean "confusion" or "haphazard" and *assault* shifting to mean "insult" or "demoralise"](http://www.esocialsciences.org/essh/Repository/7_Loanword%20Adaptation_Moumita%20Singha.pdf). *Propose* narrowing from "ask to marry" to "ask to be together" is the same kind of event, on a word that happens to carry a whole calendar day with it.

## The date, briefly: Monday 8 February 2027

Propose Day 2027 is **Monday 8 February**, the second of the eight dated days of Valentine week, which runs Sunday 7 February (Rose Day) to Sunday 14 February (Valentine's Day). It is a working Monday, not the Sunday it fell on in 2026. The calendar and what a working Monday does to timing are covered in the companion post on `propose-day-2027`; this page is about the word.

## Four things "propose karna" can mean

Each entry gives the Hindi, a literal reading, the register it assumes, and what to send. Register sits on the pronoun: तू is intimate or non-honorific, तुम familiar, आप respectful — a four-way conjugation split in standard Hindustani grammar, and the error a native reader notices first.

### 1. Saying it for the first time

**The Hindi:** मुझे तुमसे प्यार है (*Mujhe tumse pyār hai*).
**Literally:** "To me, from you, there is love" — "I love you."
**Register:** तुम, familiar. With आप it becomes मुझे आपसे प्यार है, which reads formal and is unusual between peers.
**What to send:** a declaration, not a question. This is what most people mean by "propose karna" and it needs no yes-or-no button.

### 2. Asking for the relationship

**The Hindi:** क्या तुम मेरी गर्लफ्रेंड बनोगी? (*Kyā tum merī girlfriend banogī?*).
**Literally:** "Will you become my girlfriend?" — the feminine future ending -ogī; a male addressee takes बनोगे (*banoge*) with बॉयफ्रेंड.
**Register:** तुम, familiar. This is the core Propose Day ask.
**What to send:** something that can receive an answer; a question left hanging in a chat thread is worse than none.

### 3. Asking for marriage, marked explicitly

**The Hindi:** क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी? (*Kyā tum mujhse śādī karogī?*).
**Literally:** "Will you do marriage with me?" — again the feminine -ogī; करोगे for a male addressee, करेंगी with आप.
**Register:** तुम here, आप where the relationship or the family setting calls for it.
**What to send:** the marriage question, and it should be unmistakable — this is the sense English-language pages assume and Hindi speakers have to mark.

### 4. रिश्ता — the proposal that is not this verb

**The Hindi:** उनका रिश्ता आया है (*Unkā riśtā āyā hai*).
**Literally:** "Their match has come" — the arranged-marriage proposal, arriving between families rather than being made by a person.
**Register:** आप-level, because it is about families. Never phrased with प्रपोज़ करना.
**What to send:** nothing from this page. This is a different social event with its own vocabulary.

## Which sense goes with which page

Two SubhSandesh templates sit on opposite sides of this split, and the irony is worth stating: the [Will You Marry Me? proposal scrapbook](/proposal) is built for the *British and American* sense — a story ending in a YES button — while most people searching this phrase mean the Indian one. For them the honest match is the ["I love you" page](/love-gf), which declares rather than asks.

If the real ask is a first date, the [invitation page](/date-invitation) fits better than either.

| What you actually mean | Hindi phrasing | Page that fits | First-party signal (platform-wide, 20 page types) |
|---|---|---|---|
| "I love you" — a confession | मुझे तुमसे प्यार है | `/love-gf` | 1,173 built, 23.2% of all pages; 16,902 views, 30.1% of all views |
| "Be my girlfriend" — the relationship ask | क्या तुम मेरी गर्लफ्रेंड बनोगी? | `/love-gf` | Same template; most-built romantic page type on the platform |
| "Will you marry me?" — the marriage ask | क्या तुम मुझसे शादी करोगी? | `/proposal` | Not published among the top five page types; no proposal-specific figure exists |
| "Come out with me" — an invitation | चलो कहीं चलते हैं | `/date-invitation` | Not published among the top five page types |

The template ranked #2 on the platform matches the Indian sense of the verb; the one named after the English sense is not in the published top five.

## What no dictionary records, and what we could not verify

English Wiktionary's entry for *propose* lists three verb senses — to suggest a plan, to ask for a person's hand in marriage, and to intend. **None of them is labelled for India, and none covers the "ask someone to be your partner" sense this page is about.** The shift is real in usage and absent from the reference works, which is worth saying out loud rather than papering over.

We also could not find a peer-reviewed study of this specific shift. Searched, through Crossref, Europe PMC, DOAJ and CORE: *semantic shift English loanwords Hindi*, *Indian English lexical innovation*, *light verb constructions Hindi English borrowing*, *loanword semantic narrowing extension*, *Hinglish verb formation karna*, *Indianisms Indian English lexical items*, and *semantic change English words Indian English variety*. The mechanism is well documented; the individual word is not, so everything above about *propose* is an observation about usage sourced to the mechanism.

The same gap applies to the day. We found no peer-reviewed source documenting when or where Propose Day began, or documenting Valentine week's day-by-day structure as a South Asian elaboration — another writer here searched roughly twelve phrasings with the same result. This page therefore states no origin story for the day.

## When a proposal page is the wrong thing on Propose Day

If you are in the same room on 8 February, say it out loud. A link is a worse medium than a voice for a sentence this short.

A page is also wrong when the answer might be no and the exchange needs privacy. Across the platform, 38.7% of creators password-protect their page before sharing it (1,961 of 5,061) — a signal that a shared link is a semi-public object. And 48.4% of views arrive on a phone (27,185 of 56,152), so a recipient without a comfortable phone-reading habit is a poor fit.

If what you mean is sense 4 — रिश्ता — none of these pages belong near it. Nothing here is built for a conversation between families.

One limit on every number here: SubhSandesh holds no proposal-specific usage data. A read-only probe of the proposal-page collection is refused by this machine's production-read policy, so every figure above is either platform-wide across 20 page types or sampled on the template named beside it.

## Sources

- Søren Wichmann and Jan Wohlgemuth, ["Loan verbs in a typological perspective"](https://www.linguist.de/jw/Wichmann_Wohlgemuth_verb-borrowing-typology.pdf), Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, *Romanisation Worldwide* proceedings, 2005.
- Ashwini Vaidya, Owen Rambow and Martha Palmer, ["Syntactic composition and selectional preferences in Hindi Light Verb Constructions"](https://journals.colorado.edu/index.php/lilt/article/view/1419), *Linguistic Issues in Language Technology* 17, 2019 (CC BY 4.0).
- Azadeh Sharifi Moghaddam, ["A Semantic Change Model for French Loanwords in Persian"](https://journals.uni-lj.si/ala/article/view/219), *Acta Linguistica Asiatica* 3(2), 2013.
- Moumita Singha, ["Loanword Adaptation Across Time: Evidence from Midnapuri Dialect of Bangla"](http://www.esocialsciences.org/essh/Repository/7_Loanword%20Adaptation_Moumita%20Singha.pdf), eSocialSciences (eSSH).

auditReport.honestAssessment: This is a definition query with near-zero conversion, kept deliberately to price that axis, and it should be judged on impressions and on whether an answer engine lifts the semantic explanation — not on pages built. What it has that a two-line definition and a quote list do not is a mechanism: the "X karna" light-verb construction is documented, a loan-verb typology of over 60 languages names Hindi borrowing from English as an instance of it, and the 2019 LiLT paper says the same from the Hindi side — so the claim that "propose karna" is a borrowed verb with a narrowed meaning is grounded rather than asserted. It also states two absences instead of papering over them: no peer-reviewed source we found documents this sense of the word, and English Wiktionary labels none of its three senses for India. The first-party page-type mix (the 'I love you' page at 1,173 of 5,061 pages, 23.2%) is the one piece of evidence no competitor can print, and it happens to corroborate the semantic argument. What it cannot overcome: these February SERPs are an annual news cycle owned by MensXP, Zee, Webdunia, Amar Ujala and Times Now, whose authority is far above this domain's — target position 6–10, not 3. No SERP was measured for this keyword, so nothing here describes a current ranking or competitor coverage, and ranking takes months regardless.
